The Persistence of Memory. Salvador Dalí's iconic 1931 Surrealist painting features melting pocket watches draped across a barren landscape, exploring the fluidity of time and the logic of dreams. Small in size but immense in influence, it has become the most recognizable symbol of Surrealism and a meditation on the relativity of temporal experience.

Painted in 1931, it measures just 24 inches by 32 inches, yet has achieved disproportionate cultural presence as the quintessential Surrealist image. The composition depicts three soft, melting watches and one rigid pocket watch covered in ants, set against a dreamlike landscape with cliffs and distorted forms. The soft watches suggest the malleability of time in the unconscious mind, contrasting with the rigidity of measured, rational time represented by the hard watch.

Dalí termed his method paranoiac-critical, a technique for accessing the unconscious by deliberately inducing paranoid-hallucinatory states to paint dream-logic. The landscape includes a distorted humanoid form often read as a self-portrait of Dalí asleep, and a cliffside suggesting the coast near Dalí's home in Catalonia. Now housed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, it has become so iconic that it is endlessly parodied and referenced in popular culture.
